findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The global cleanup job interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This looks like a leftover debugging change. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often. The annotation cleanup is the one that contends with inserts, so this raises the chance of the deadlock the PR is meant to fix. It is also unrelated to the PR description and should be reverted.

findings.title: Debug logging at Error level that dumps all IDs on every batch
findings.body: Each batch calls `r.log.Error(...)` with the full `ids` slice (up to the batch size, which may be tens of thousands), the condition and the result. The same pattern appears at lines 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579. These are routine events, not errors, so the log will fill with error-level entries. Dumping huge ID lists on every batch bloats logs and falsely triggers error alerting. Remove them or use Debug without the ID list. The `err` logged right after the `err != nil` check is also always nil.

findings.title: SQLite parameter-limit workaround keyed on batch size config instead of len(ids)
findings.body: The inline-IDs path is chosen from `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999` rather than from the number of IDs actually being deleted. It also hardcodes 999, although newer SQLite builds allow 32766. This is functionally safe, but it builds SQL by string-concatenating the IDs, which is quadratic via repeated `fmt.Sprintf` for tens of thousands of IDs. Use a `strings.Builder`, or chunk the deletes into groups under the limit and always use placeholders. Other drivers also have limits: MySQL allows 65535 placeholders and Postgres allows 65535 bind parameters. A batch size above those would fail on those databases.

findings.title: Orphaned tag cleanup fetches IDs in a way that can loop forever or stay slow
findings.body: In `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags`, `fetchIDs` selects `id` from `annotation_tag` with `NOT EXISTS (... WHERE annotation_id = a.id)` and no ORDER BY. The condition is built as `WHERE NOT EXISTS (...) LIMIT n`. That is valid, but the subquery's unqualified `annotation_id` and `a.id` rely on scoping, so it is fragile. More importantly, the delete count now depends on `RowsAffected` from a separate statement. If the loop's only termination is `affected == 0`, a delete that affects fewer rows than fetched (concurrent deletion) is fine, but a delete that persistently affects zero while IDs are still returned ends the loop early. This leaves orphans, but they are cleaned next cycle, so it is low impact.

findings.title: Condition string built with raw annotationType and ORDER BY/LIMIT concatenation; MaxCount path semantic
findings.body: `fetchIDs` appends the condition as a raw string (`WHERE %s`). The callers embed `annotationType` and the ORDER BY/LIMIT clause into it. `fetchIDs` therefore isn't a reusable, safe helper: any condition lacking the right structure produces broken SQL. `LimitOffset` with a changing offset is correct only because deleted rows shift the window. If a delete partially fails to affect rows, the same IDs are re-fetched on each pass.

findings.title: Large-batch test inserts 40k rows with explicit IDs into a shared DB and does not exercise MySQL/non-SQLite paths
findings.body: The new case sets explicit `ID: int64(i+1)` on annotations, which in this test conflicts with prior leftover rows only if cleanup is incomplete. It also only verifies the SQLite large-batch path. There is no test for the actual deadlock scenario (concurrent inserts during cleanup), nor for `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` with large batches. The test names say SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER, but the fallback threshold used in code is 999, so the 32767 case only checks the inline-ID path.
